ladder:ai:100.rationale: This rung asks only for one hundred deaths or two hundred twenty million dollars in damages summed across all artificial-intelligence-related incidents starting inside the window, and the dollar branch is already being cleared in the ordinary course of business: recorded deepfake-fraud losses were about two and a half billion dollars globally in 2025 and another seven hundred sixty-four million dollars in the first half of 2026, and the International Business Machines 2026 breach study found that one in four malicious breaches were artificial-intelligence-enabled at an average cost of about six million dollars each. Even under a stricter reading that demands one identifiable campaign, individual criminal operations of the size documented in 2026 (a reported campaign against three hundred ninety-five organisations, large deepfake investment-scam networks) plausibly reach two hundred twenty million dollars on their own, so I gave the strict reading roughly one-fifth weight and still landed near the top of the scale. Longer horizons rise only slightly because the probability is already close to one, leaving little room for policy or capability conditions to move it.

key_sources.contribution: share and average cost of artificial-intelligence-enabled breaches, giving the per-incident dollar scale
year-by-year recorded global deepfake fraud losses used as the aggregation base
expert medians on how much artificial intelligence adds to reported cybercrime losses

ladder:ai:100.weakest_link: That whoever resolves the question will genuinely add up damages across many separate artificial-intelligence-related incidents rather than insisting on one concentrated, well-documented event.

ladder:ai:1k.rationale: One thousand deaths or two point two billion dollars in cumulative damages is still reached mainly through money, not bodies: reported global fraud losses are running in the hundreds of billions of dollars per year with artificial intelligence named by Interpol as the industrialising force, and the Forecasting Research Institute's expert panel expects artificial intelligence to add roughly twenty-four billion dollars per year to United States reported cybercrime losses by 2031 relative to a slow-progress world. Summed over a six- to twelve-month onset window, with each incident's harms counted for three years, the two point two billion dollar figure is likely; a single campaign of that size is much less likely in the near term, so blending the loose and strict readings pulls the short-horizon numbers down from near-certainty. By the late 2020s and beyond both readings converge upward, which is why the curve flattens near the top.

key_sources.contribution: expert forecasts of reported cybercrime losses under fast versus slow artificial-intelligence progress
Interpol's four hundred forty-two billion dollar global fraud estimate attributed partly to artificial intelligence
documented growth of artificial-intelligence-enabled criminal operations including the first agentic ransomware case

ladder:ai:1k.weakest_link: The counterfactual test - that these losses would not have occurred, or would have been far smaller, without artificial intelligence - is asserted by industry reports rather than measured.

ladder:ai:10k.rationale: Twenty-two billion dollars of cumulative damage is the level at which the answer stops being automatic and starts depending on how broadly harm is aggregated. If the resolver adds up all artificial-intelligence-attributable fraud, ransomware, remediation and lost output worldwide, current trajectories (a few billion dollars per year of recorded deepfake fraud, plus the roughly one million dollar extra cost per artificial-intelligence-enabled breach across a very large number of breaches) reach twenty-two billion within a year or two; if the resolver wants one campaign of that size, it is unlikely before the 2030s, since the largest single confirmed events to date are far smaller. I weighted the broad reading about two-thirds, which gives roughly a one-in-three chance within six months rising to high probability by 2050.

key_sources.contribution: quantified gap between fast and slow artificial-intelligence worlds in reported cybercrime losses
explicit warning that aggregate annual cybercrime losses cannot be used as a single-campaign loss figure
per-incident cost premium for artificial-intelligence-driven attacks and their growth rate
share of organisations reporting incidents involving artificial-intelligence systems

ladder:ai:10k.weakest_link: The split I assumed between the aggregate reading and the single-campaign reading is a guess about resolver behaviour, and the answer at this rung is very sensitive to it.

ladder:ai:100k.rationale: Two hundred twenty billion dollars, or one hundred thousand deaths, requires either a systemic event - a prolonged outage of payments, power or telecommunications - or many years of accumulating diffuse artificial-intelligence-attributable losses. For the concentrated route I leaned on the takeoff.watch cyber ladder, which puts a confirmed national-scale artificial-intelligence-executed event at roughly half by 2031 and a mass-harm event (one hundred deaths or ten billion dollars in one campaign) at only twelve to twenty percent, and on the fact that no artificial-intelligence-caused event has yet produced even a day-long outage at a named victim. For the diffuse route, projections such as Deloitte's forty billion dollars per year of United States generative-artificial-intelligence fraud by 2027 make two hundred twenty billion cumulative plausible in the 2030s and 2040s, which is why my numbers climb steeply after 2030.

key_sources.contribution: rung-by-rung probabilities for national-scale and mass-harm artificial-intelligence-executed cyber events through 2031
Deloitte projection of generative-artificial-intelligence fraud losses reaching forty billion dollars per year
expert view that a major artificial-intelligence harm event is more likely than not by 2050

ladder:ai:100k.weakest_link: Whether damages from very many small, independent artificial-intelligence-enabled frauds would ever be summed into a two-hundred-billion-dollar figure by an expert panel.

ladder:ai:1M.rationale: At one million deaths or two point two trillion dollars, the dollar branch is equivalent to roughly two percent of one year of world output and the death branch is roughly one-eighth of the threshold the catastrophe questions use. I treated this as mostly a concentrated-event question - a mass-casualty engineered outbreak, a prolonged infrastructure collapse, or artificial-intelligence-driven warfare - and anchored on the Forecasting Research Institute expert panel, whose median for an artificial-intelligence catastrophe killing more than ten percent of humanity was one percent by 2030 and five percent by 2050 in a fast-progress world. Because this rung sits well below that threshold and admits an economic route, I set it several times higher than those catastrophe numbers, with most of the probability arriving after 2030 as autonomous systems reach infrastructure, weapons and biology.

key_sources.contribution: median expert probabilities for artificial-intelligence catastrophes by 2030, 2050 and 2100 under fast progress
Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament medians for artificial-intelligence catastrophic risk (about two percent for superforecasters, twelve percent for domain experts by 2100)
judgement that the hundred-death and ten-billion-dollar routes are narrower than media descriptions suggest

ladder:ai:1M.weakest_link: That the expert medians I anchored on, elicited before the most recent capability jump, still describe the risk in a world where a frontier developer declares critical cyber capability.

ladder:ai:10M.rationale: Ten million deaths or twenty-two trillion dollars is a genuine global disaster - about the scale of the COVID-19 pandemic in deaths and larger in money - and reaching it needs a self-propagating mechanism: an engineered pandemic, a nuclear exchange triggered or enabled by artificial intelligence, or a sustained loss of industrial civilisation's control systems. My anchor is the Forecasting Research Institute panel's five percent for an artificial-intelligence catastrophe killing over ten percent of humanity by 2050 in a fast-progress world, scaled up because ten million is roughly eighty times smaller than that threshold, and the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament spread between superforecasters and domain experts. Almost all of the probability lands after 2030; the six- and twelve-month figures reflect that no currently deployed system has the physical reach to do this.

key_sources.contribution: fast-versus-slow-progress medians for artificial-intelligence-related global catastrophe
benchmark catastrophic-risk medians from a large forecasting tournament
current status of biological capability thresholds, the most plausible route to this death toll

ladder:ai:10M.weakest_link: The scaling step from a one-in-twenty chance of an eight-hundred-million-death catastrophe to a probability for a ten-million-death event is a judgement about the shape of the severity distribution, not something the sources measure.

ladder:ai:100M.rationale: One hundred million deaths is within a factor of about eight of the ten-percent-of-humanity threshold used by the separate catastrophe question, so I pinned this rung just above my artificial-intelligence catastrophe numbers and kept the two internally consistent. The mechanism is essentially the catastrophe mechanism: a deliberately engineered pathogen with artificial-intelligence assistance, artificial intelligence triggering or enabling nuclear use, or an autonomous system pursuing goals at civilisational scale. The Forecasting Research Institute panel's ten percent by 2100 under fast progress, and the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's twelve percent for domain experts versus about two percent for superforecasters, bracket where I sat.

key_sources.contribution: median artificial-intelligence catastrophe probabilities that set the level for this rung
expert versus superforecaster range for artificial-intelligence catastrophic risk
evidence that nuclear risk pathways, which artificial intelligence could couple to, are worsening

ladder:ai:100M.weakest_link: Treating expert medians about a hypothetical ten-percent-mortality catastrophe as transferable to a one-hundred-million-death threshold with a simple offset.

ladder:ai:1B.rationale: One billion deaths is slightly above the ten-percent-of-world-population threshold used by the catastrophe question, so I set this rung just below my artificial-intelligence catastrophe figures and above artificial-intelligence extinction. Only a small set of mechanisms scale this far - a highly transmissible engineered pathogen, a full nuclear exchange with its aftermath, or an artificial intelligence pursuing objectives incompatible with large human populations - and each of those requires capabilities well beyond what the September 2026 frontier demonstrates. The Forecasting Research Institute panel's ten percent for a fast-progress world by 2100 and the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's three percent domain-expert extinction figure gave me the ceiling and floor to interpolate between.

key_sources.contribution: catastrophe probabilities at the ten-percent-mortality level that bound this rung from above
extinction-level medians that bound this rung from below
forecast that an artificial-intelligence system surviving a shutdown attempt may be confirmed within five years, relevant to loss-of-control pathways

ladder:ai:1B.weakest_link: The assumption that severity falls off smoothly between the hundred-million and extinction rungs, when many plausible scenarios are all-or-nothing.

ladder:ai:extinction.rationale: Human extinction, defined here as the global population falling below five thousand, requires an artificial intelligence with autonomous physical reach, a self-replicating weapon, or control of nuclear arsenals, and nothing in the 2026 record comes close - the most severe confirmed autonomy incidents involved agents breaching a software repository and creating fake online identities, with no physical harm. I anchored on the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, where superforecasters gave about zero point four percent and domain experts about three percent for artificial-intelligence extinction by 2100, and on the usual expert ratio in which extinction is roughly a quarter of catastrophe risk applied to the Forecasting Research Institute's ten percent fast-progress catastrophe figure. That puts me near the domain-expert end at about three percent by 2100, with the near-term horizons orders of magnitude lower because the causal chain cannot plausibly complete within months.

key_sources.contribution: the two reference numbers for artificial-intelligence extinction risk by 2100
fast-progress catastrophe medians from which I derived an extinction share
concrete evidence of how limited real-world autonomous agent harm still is

ladder:ai:extinction.weakest_link: The habit of treating extinction as a fixed fraction of catastrophe risk, which may badly misdescribe scenarios where a system powerful enough to kill a billion people is also powerful enough to finish the job.

ladder:bio:100.rationale: For an artificial-intelligence-related human-caused epidemic to cause one hundred deaths or two hundred twenty million dollars of damage, someone must use artificial intelligence to design, enhance or acquire a pathogen and then release it, deliberately or accidentally, with enough spread to kill at scale or trigger a costly public-health response. Nothing like this has ever happened: no biological attack in history has killed one hundred people (the 2001 anthrax letters killed five while costing over a billion dollars in decontamination), and as of September 2026 the takeoff.watch tracker puts a government-confirmed case of artificial intelligence materially enabling an actual synthesis at thirty-four to fifty-six percent by 2031 and a linked release killing ten or more people at only seven to eleven percent. I used that seven-to-eleven percent as my anchor for the early 2030s, kept the near-term numbers under one percent, and let the curve rise steeply to the middle of the century as capability spreads to open-weight and foreign models.

key_sources.contribution: explicit probabilities for artificial-intelligence-enabled synthesis and for a release causing ten or more deaths by 2031
assessment of the practical wet-laboratory hurdles that remain after information uplift
evidence that language-model agents can already operate biological design tools, lowering the expertise barrier
developer statement that its models are close to the novel chemical and biological weapons threshold

ladder:bio:100.weakest_link: That the tacit laboratory skills needed to turn digital design help into a spreading pathogen remain a hard barrier, which is exactly what the next capability generation might erode.

ladder:bio:1k.rationale: One thousand deaths or two point two billion dollars is only modestly harder than the hundred-level rung, because almost any engineered outbreak that spreads beyond a handful of cases will cost more than two point two billion dollars in response and lost output - the 2022 mpox emergency and comparable regional outbreaks cost in that range. So I set this rung at roughly two-thirds of the hundred-level rung rather than an order of magnitude below it, and kept the same underlying driver: the chance that anyone uses artificial intelligence to create and release a pathogen at all, which the takeoff.watch tracker puts at seven to eleven percent for a ten-death release by 2031. The long-horizon numbers grow because both capability diffusion and the number of potential actors grow, while gene-synthesis screening remains voluntary and incomplete in the United States.

key_sources.contribution: base probability of any artificial-intelligence-linked release with casualties
finding that the United States has no comprehensive biosecurity statute beyond the select-agent programme
overview of developer safeguards and pending legislation as of September 2026

ladder:bio:1k.weakest_link: The assumption that an engineered outbreak large enough to kill a thousand people would be recognised and costed as artificial-intelligence-caused rather than as a natural emergence.

ladder:bio:10k.rationale: Ten thousand deaths requires a pathogen that actually transmits between humans reasonably well, which is a much stronger requirement than the toxin or non-contagious agent scenarios most accessible to a small actor. My reference points are that no deliberate biological attack has ever reached this toll, that the worst plausible laboratory-origin comparison (the 1977 influenza re-emergence) is contested, and that Anthropic's own risk report says its models are close to but have not crossed the novel chemical and biological weapons threshold, with the tracker putting the top-tier capability declaration at roughly eighty percent by 2031 while the harm rungs stay far lower. I therefore kept near-term numbers at a fraction of a percent and let the 2050 and 2100 figures rise into the teens and twenties as both capability and the pool of capable actors widen.

key_sources.contribution: the large gap between capability-threshold declarations and actual casualty events
developer assessment of proximity to the novel biological weapons capability threshold
empirical testing of language-model agents operating biological tools

ladder:bio:10k.weakest_link: That transmissibility remains the binding constraint - if artificial intelligence delivers reliable design of transmissible agents, this rung and the ones above it move together and quickly.

ladder:bio:100k.rationale: At one hundred thousand deaths or two hundred twenty billion dollars we are in pandemic territory rather than attack territory, so the scenario is a deliberately engineered, human-transmissible pathogen released widely enough to seed global spread. Historical anchors are thin and all natural: the 1957 and 1968 influenza pandemics each killed on the order of one to four million people, and COVID-19 killed several million reported, so a deliberate event of this size is unprecedented. I priced it as a modest fraction of the hundred-death rung, with the ratio narrowing over time because the same capability that enables any release increasingly enables a transmissible one, and because published expert panels (272 international experts in the 2026 Delphi study) put double-digit probabilities on catastrophic weapons-and-cyberattack outcomes over five-year windows, which I treated as an upper bound rather than a central estimate given their loose threshold definition.

key_sources.contribution: expert Delphi probabilities for catastrophic weapons and cyberattack outcomes by 2030
casualty-rung probabilities that anchor the low end
catastrophe-level medians constraining how high biological rungs can go

ladder:bio:100k.weakest_link: The 2026 Delphi study's definition of catastrophic harm bundles one million deaths with one hundred billion dollars of loss, so its double-digit numbers cannot be read directly as death-threshold probabilities and I may have leaned on them too loosely.

ladder:bio:1M.rationale: A million deaths from a deliberately created pathogen is roughly the scale of a severe natural influenza pandemic, and the only realistic route is an engineered agent that is both lethal and transmissible, released by a state programme, a well-resourced group, or by accident from such work. I anchored on the Forecasting Research Institute's fast-progress artificial-intelligence catastrophe medians of five percent by 2050 and ten percent by 2100 for events eight hundred times larger, then worked downward in severity and upward in probability, cross-checked against the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's engineered-pathogen numbers where domain experts sat near a few percent for catastrophic outcomes by 2100. That produced low single-digit percentages by mid-century and low double digits by 2100, with almost nothing in the next two years.

key_sources.contribution: catastrophe-scale medians used as the upper anchor
tournament estimates for engineered-pathogen catastrophe and extinction risk
current absence of any confirmed artificial-intelligence-enabled biological incident

ladder:bio:1M.weakest_link: The share of future biological catastrophe risk that counts as artificial-intelligence-related under the but-for test, which I assumed is large and rising but cannot verify.

ladder:bio:10M.rationale: Ten million deaths is COVID-19-scale or worse and would require an engineered pathogen that evades early containment globally, which combines the hardest technical requirement with the hardest operational one. With no historical precedent for a deliberate event at this level, I derived the numbers by scaling down from the ten-percent-of-humanity catastrophe estimates - five percent by 2050 and ten percent by 2100 in the Forecasting Research Institute's fast-progress scenario - and attributing the larger part of long-run biological catastrophe risk to artificial-intelligence-assisted pathogens, since that is where expert commentary now locates the growth. The result is a few percent by 2050 and high single digits by 2100, with essentially nothing in the first two years.

key_sources.contribution: the catastrophe-level medians I scaled from
evidence that even ten-death artificial-intelligence-linked releases remain unlikely this decade
sceptical treatment of how far information uplift translates into mass-casualty capability

ladder:bio:10M.weakest_link: Assuming the ratio between a ten-million-death event and an eight-hundred-million-death event is stable over eighty years, when pandemic containment capability may change dramatically in either direction.

ladder:bio:100M.rationale: One hundred million deaths from a human-caused epidemic would be the deadliest event in human history in absolute terms, comparable in proportion to the 1918 influenza pandemic, and needs a pathogen deliberately optimised for both lethality and spread plus a failure of global containment. I set this rung just below my artificial-intelligence catastrophe numbers at each horizon, treating engineered biology as the single most plausible route to that catastrophe level, consistent with the Forecasting Research Institute panel's ten percent fast-progress figure by 2100 for events of roughly eight times this size. The near-term numbers are tiny because the capability thresholds that developers themselves monitor have not been crossed as of September 2026.

key_sources.contribution: upper anchor for catastrophe-scale artificial-intelligence outcomes
current state of the novel biological weapons capability threshold
timeline for when that threshold is expected to be declared crossed

ladder:bio:100M.weakest_link: That a pathogen capable of killing a hundred million people would stop there rather than cascading into the higher rungs, which makes the ordering between this rung and the next partly arbitrary.

ladder:bio:1B.rationale: A billion deaths from an engineered epidemic is above the ten-percent-of-population catastrophe threshold and effectively requires a deliberately optimised agent plus the collapse of medical and food systems in its wake. My numbers come from taking the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's engineered-pathogen catastrophe estimates (a few percent for domain experts by 2100, far lower for superforecasters) and the Forecasting Research Institute's fast-progress catastrophe medians, then assigning the biological share of that risk. Everything before 2030 is negligible because the enabling capability is not present and no state or group is known to be pursuing an agent of this kind with artificial-intelligence assistance.

key_sources.contribution: engineered-pathogen catastrophe and extinction medians from experts and superforecasters
fast-progress catastrophe medians for artificial-intelligence-related events
review showing limited regional resilience to global catastrophic biological risk

ladder:bio:1B.weakest_link: The deep disagreement between superforecasters and domain experts at this severity - two orders of magnitude - means my point estimates are a weighted opinion, not a measurement.

ladder:bio:extinction.rationale: Extinction by engineered pandemic requires a pathogen with near-universal lethality and transmission, or several released together, plus the failure of every isolated human population - a combination most biologists regard as extraordinarily difficult even deliberately. The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's engineered-pathogen extinction medians were about one percent for domain experts and about one in ten thousand for superforecasters by 2100; I sat closer to the expert end but below one percent, because artificial intelligence plausibly raises design capability while detection, sequencing surveillance and medical countermeasures also improve. The short horizons are essentially zero on this pathway.

key_sources.contribution: the two anchor estimates for engineered-pathogen extinction risk by 2100
current absence of any confirmed artificial-intelligence-material biological synthesis
assessment of how poorly prepared regions are for global catastrophic biological risk

ladder:bio:extinction.weakest_link: Whether defensive capability (rapid sequencing, countermeasure design, isolation) scales with offensive capability, which drives whether this number is one in a thousand or one in a hundred.

ladder:cyber:100.rationale: Artificial-intelligence-enabled cyber operations are already causing losses at this scale continuously: Surfshark recorded about two and a half billion dollars of global deepfake fraud in 2025 and another seven hundred sixty-four million in the first half of 2026, Interpol reports that more than half of cybercrime in Africa is now artificial-intelligence-enabled, and the International Business Machines study found artificial-intelligence-enabled breaches cost about six million dollars each on average. Summing campaigns whose onset falls in even a six-month window clears two hundred twenty million dollars with room to spare; a single named campaign of that size is also plausible given documented multi-hundred-victim agentic operations, so both readings point the same way. My numbers stay just short of certainty only because of residual ambiguity about whether the resolver requires each campaign's artificial-intelligence contribution to have been counterfactually necessary.

key_sources.contribution: year-by-year recorded deepfake fraud losses globally
Interpol finding that fifty-five percent of reported African cybercrime involves artificial intelligence
per-breach cost of artificial-intelligence-enabled attacks and their year-on-year growth

ladder:cyber:100.weakest_link: That recorded fraud statistics, which are self-reported and partly promotional, survive a strict but-for causation test applied by an expert panel.

ladder:cyber:1k.rationale: Two point two billion dollars cumulative is roughly one year of currently recorded global deepfake fraud, so the aggregate reading clears it quickly; the strict single-campaign reading is harder, since the largest individually documented artificial-intelligence-enabled incident so far is on the order of tens of millions of dollars. I blended the two, weighting aggregation about three-quarters, and used the Forecasting Research Institute panel's projection that United States reported cyber-enabled crime losses rise from about twenty-one billion dollars in 2025 to thirty-one billion in 2026 and fifty billion by 2028 under fast artificial-intelligence progress as the growth path. That yields two-thirds or better within six months, climbing toward near-certainty by the 2030s.

key_sources.contribution: expert projections of reported cybercrime losses under fast and slow artificial-intelligence progress
the current annual run-rate of recorded artificial-intelligence-specific fraud losses
evidence on ransom sizes, no-code ransomware kits and the first agentic ransomware case

ladder:cyber:1k.weakest_link: The weighting between the cumulative and single-campaign readings, which is my inference about resolution practice rather than something stated in the question.

ladder:cyber:10k.rationale: Twenty-two billion dollars is larger than any single confirmed cyber event in history including NotPetya, so this rung depends on whether the resolver sums many artificial-intelligence-enabled campaigns. The Forecasting Research Institute panel's gap between fast and slow progress worlds - roughly twenty-four billion dollars per year of extra United States reported losses by 2031 - suggests the aggregate figure crosses this level within a year or two, while takeoff.watch explicitly cautions that aggregate annual cybercrime losses must not be treated as a single-campaign figure and puts a confirmed single mass-harm artificial-intelligence-executed campaign (one hundred deaths or ten billion dollars) at only twelve to twenty percent by 2031. Blending those gave roughly one chance in four within six months, rising past a half by 2028.

key_sources.contribution: explicit rung probabilities and the warning against using aggregate losses as single-campaign damage
size of the artificial-intelligence-attributable increment in reported cybercrime losses
confirmation that artificial-intelligence-assisted reconnaissance is now aimed at industrial control systems

ladder:cyber:10k.weakest_link: That global artificial-intelligence-attributable cyber damages can be credibly estimated at all, given that reporting is partial and attribution is contested even with perfect knowledge assumed.

ladder:cyber:100k.rationale: Two hundred twenty billion dollars, or one hundred thousand deaths, from cyber operations means either a long systemic outage of payments, power, water or telecommunications, or decades of accumulated artificial-intelligence-attributable losses. On the concentrated route, takeoff.watch puts a critical-infrastructure service disruption at about seventy percent and a national-scale artificial-intelligence-executed event at about half by 2031, but a single ten-billion-dollar loss at only twelve to twenty percent, and the largest historical reinsurance scenarios for a global coordinated attack sit at eighty-five to one hundred ninety-three billion dollars. On the diffuse route, the Deloitte projection of forty billion dollars per year of United States generative-artificial-intelligence fraud by 2027 makes this level reachable in the 2030s, which is where my curve turns up sharply.

key_sources.contribution: probabilities for critical-infrastructure disruption, national-scale and mass-harm artificial-intelligence cyber events
insurance-modelled damage range for a coordinated global cyberattack, showing what scale is physically plausible
Deloitte projection of generative-artificial-intelligence fraud growth

ladder:cyber:100k.weakest_link: Whether an expert panel would count multi-year, economy-wide fraud aggregates toward a two-hundred-twenty-billion-dollar threshold, or demand one catastrophic campaign.

ladder:cyber:1M.rationale: One million deaths or two point two trillion dollars from cyber operations essentially requires a prolonged loss of critical infrastructure - months without electricity, water treatment or medical supply chains in populous regions - since cyberattacks kill indirectly. Nothing remotely like this has occurred; the worst real cases (Colonial Pipeline in 2021, Change Healthcare and the National Health Service pathology provider in 2024) caused days-to-weeks of disruption and no mass mortality, and takeoff.watch judges even a one-hundred-death confirmed artificial-intelligence-executed campaign to be a low-probability tail through 2031. I therefore kept near-term numbers well under one percent and allowed growth into the tens of percent only by 2050 and 2100, as autonomous offensive agents proliferate into operational technology environments.

key_sources.contribution: assessment that the hundred-death route is the narrowest and slowest to be confirmed
current federal warnings about artificial-intelligence-assisted targeting of water, energy and chemical control systems
framing of prolonged infrastructure loss as a distinct global catastrophic pathway

ladder:cyber:1M.weakest_link: The link from a long infrastructure outage to mass mortality is modelled, not observed, and the death toll per month of outage could be far lower or higher than I assumed.

ladder:cyber:10M.rationale: Ten million deaths or twenty-two trillion dollars through cyber means implies civilisation-scale infrastructure collapse sustained long enough for famine and disease to take hold, or a cyber-triggered military catastrophe. The reference class is empty: no cyberattack has ever killed more than a handful of people even indirectly, and the published tail estimates for coordinated global attacks top out near two hundred billion dollars. My numbers are therefore small-tail judgements that grow with the spread of autonomous offensive agents into physical systems and with the possibility of cyber operations coupling to nuclear or military escalation, reaching high single digits to low tens of percent only at the 2050 and 2100 horizons.

key_sources.contribution: tail-risk framing for artificial-intelligence-executed mass-harm cyber events over five years
upper bound from insurance modelling of a global coordinated attack
evidence that escalation thresholds are being lowered, which is the main route from cyber to mass casualties

ladder:cyber:10M.weakest_link: Assigning any specific number to an event class with zero historical instances and no accepted model of cascading infrastructure mortality.

ladder:cyber:100M.rationale: At one hundred million deaths the cyber pathway is really a proxy for cyber operations triggering something else - a nuclear exchange, a collapse of global food and energy logistics, or an artificial intelligence using cyber means as one arm of a broader takeover. I priced it as a small fraction of my overall artificial-intelligence catastrophe estimate, since the Forecasting Research Institute panel's fast-progress figure of ten percent by 2100 for ten-percent-of-humanity catastrophes covers all mechanisms and cyber is only one of them, and because most catastrophe scenarios experts describe run through biology or autonomous systems rather than pure cyber. Near-term numbers are negligible.

key_sources.contribution: overall artificial-intelligence catastrophe medians from which I carved out the cyber share

===== MISALIGNED AI INCIDENT =====

--- ladder:misalign:100 (severity: 100 deaths or $220M) ---
What is the probability that one or more Misaligned AI incidents cumulatively causes 100 deaths (or equivalent morbidity) or $220 million in economic damages within 6 months / within 12 months / by the end of 2028 / by the end of 2030 / by the end of 2050 / by the end of 2100?
Horizons for this question: 6mo, 12mo, 2028, 2030, 2050, 2100

Resolution criteria:
* An incident in which an AI system behaves in a way that neither its developer nor its operating user intended or endorsed. This "neither" reading is deliberate and separates loss of control from misuse:  
    * Excluded (misuse): a user intentionally directs an AI to cause harm and it complies. The user's intent is served even if the developer's is not. If such an event involves a cyber attack, it belongs under the Cyber questions.  
    * Included (loss of control): the AI pursues objectives, takes actions, or produces outputs that diverge from what both the developer and the operating user wanted — e.g., an autonomous agent taking destructive actions no one authorized, specification-gaming with large real-world costs, or deceptive or manipulative behavior neither party sought.  
  * Boundary with ordinary failure: the incident should center on the AI system's own behavior or decision-making being the proximate cause, rather than a conventional software defect or an operator error. This line is not crisp; use your judgment and assume the perfect-knowledge clause lets us determine whether the AI was acting contrary to both parties' intent versus functioning as designed.  
  * The harm may arise from the AI acting directly, or from actions humans took in direct reliance on the AI's misaligned outputs; in either case the AI's behavior must be the proximate driver.

===== CROSS-CUTTING =====

--- catastrophe:general (severity: deaths reaching 10% of the population) ---
What is the probability that any global catastrophe (deaths reaching at least 10% of the population alive at the start of the measurement window) will occur within 6 months / within 12 months / by the end of 2028 / by the end of 2030 / by the end of 2050 / by the end of 2100?
Horizons for this question: 6mo, 12mo, 2028, 2030, 2050, 2100

Resolution criteria:
* Catastrophe threshold and the measurement window: A catastrophe at the 10% level means that deaths attributable to the catastrophe (excess mortality, i.e., deaths beyond the baseline that would have occurred anyway) reach at least 10% of the population alive at the start of the measurement window.  
* The measurement window is any contiguous period of at most five years during which the attributable deaths accumulate to the threshold. The window must begin on or after December 31, 2025 and end on or before December 31 of the resolution year (2030, 2050, or 2100). A faster event; the five years is a ceiling on the span over which deaths are counted, not a required duration.  
* For a threshold to resolve positively, the deaths must arise from a single catastrophe or a single causally-linked chain of events, not from summing unrelated causes.  
* Data and disagreement: For fatality and population data, we will rely on broadly recognized sources (e.g., Our World in Data, the Economist, the United Nations). Where these disagree in ways that would change resolution, we will resolve by the majority opinion of a panel of experts in demographics and fields relevant to the specific catastrophe (e.g., epidemiology for a pandemic). If reasonable people disagree about whether the event occurred, the question resolves via the same expert panel.
* [Scope of "the resolution year", added 2026-08-28 when these questions moved onto the incident ladder's horizon grid: read it as the resolution date of whichever horizon you are answering, which for a rolling horizon is that many months after today's date. The rule is otherwise unchanged -- the measurement window still begins on or after December 31, 2025, must end on or before that resolution date, and still spans at most five years.]

Perfect Knowledge:
* Perfect-knowledge clause: Assume we have perfect knowledge of the cause of each event, the intent and identity of the actors involved (including whether an AI system was involved and in what role), and the technical attribution. We want your view on the damages resulting from these events, not on the probability that they would be correctly identified or attributed.  
* Incident categories could overlap; for example, a misaligned AI incident could also be counted as an AI-related cyber incident, provided such an incident met the defined thresholds for each category.

Severity:
* The figure of [X] deaths refers to global excess mortality that is believed to be attributed to the incident(s).   
  * The deaths do not need to be directly attributed to the incident but if there is an alternative reason for excess mortality to increase in a location (e.g. due to conflict) then the excess mortality for that region will not be counted as deaths as a result of the incident. E.g., famine deaths that would not have occurred absent the incident would count, while deaths due to a conflict that likely would have occurred anyway would not.  
  * For this question to resolve positively, more than X million excess deaths attributable to the incident must occur within a 3-year period, beginning from the onset of the incident.  
  * In the absence of a published estimate, we will defer to the majority opinion of a panel of at least five experts to determine if this criterion has been met.  
* Equivalent morbidity is defined as roughly 10 QALYs per death, e.g. 100 million QALYs is intended to represent morbidity roughly equivalent to 10 million deaths.  
  * A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) is a measure used in health economics that combines both the length and quality of life, where one QALY equals one year lived in perfect health. It's calculated by multiplying the number of years lived by a quality score between 0 (death) and 1 (perfect health), allowing comparison of different health interventions' effectiveness.  
  * An estimate of QALYs lost due to the pathogen that is published in a peer-reviewed journal, or by an international organization such as the World Health Organization or World Bank, would be sufficient to resolve this question.  
  * In the absence of such an estimate, we will defer to the majority opinion of a panel of at least five experts to determine if this criterion has been met.  
* Economic damages: Economic damages refer to global economic costs attributable to the event, beginning from the start of the event and extending to three years after the event onset. These include:  
  * Direct economic losses — e.g., reduced productivity and income (commonly estimated as a reduction in GDP); costs of response, remediation, recovery, and decontamination; destroyed or unrecoverable data and hardware; ransoms paid; medical and public-health response costs; regulatory penalties tied to the event.  
  * Monetized mortality, using a value of a statistical life (VSL) of $2.2 million, regardless of the geographic distribution of fatalities.  
  * Exclude purely notional losses such as declines in market capitalization or share price that do not correspond to real resource costs. Give all estimates in 2026 USD.  
* Resolution sources: Assume access to authoritative assessments, which may include estimates from the WHO, World Bank, IMF, national cybersecurity agencies (e.g., CISA, ENISA), major insurers and reinsurers, incident-response and threat-intelligence firms, and academic epidemiological and economic-modeling groups. Where multiple analyses exist, we will use the consensus or median; absent that, we will defer to the majority opinion of a panel of at least five experts.

P1. Federal Preemption on State AI Laws

Summary: A US federal statute or action barring states from regulating AI more strictly than the federal government.

Background:
Federal preemption of state AI laws has been pursued through several channels, but no cross-cutting federal AI statute or order has barred states from imposing stricter AI requirements than federal law. In Congress, a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws was [stripped](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/moratoriums-and-federal-preemption-of-state-artificial-intelligence-laws-pose-serious-risks/) from both a 2025 Senate reconciliation bill and the [Big Beautiful Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act). In March 2026, the White House’s National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence [included](https://www.ropesgray.com/en/insights/alerts/2026/03/the-white-house-legislative-recommendations-national-policy-framework-for-artificial-intelligence-an) an assertion of broad federal authority over AI laws, and an executive order passed shortly before the Framework created a task force to “challenge state laws on constitutional grounds, including preemption and the Dormant Commerce Clause.” In April 2026, the Department of Justice [intervened](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/de3ad9de/xai-sues-doj-intervenes-enforcement-of-colorado-ai-act-suspended) in a lawsuit xAI filed against a Colorado law prohibiting “algorithmic discrimination,” resulting in a federal court temporarily suspending enforcement of the law; the law was later [repealed and replaced](https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2026/06/colorado-repeals-and-replaces-its-ai-act). In June 2026, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) [released](https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2026/06/unpacking-the-great-american-ai-act) draft legislation entitled the “Great American AI Act,” which would “preempt state laws and rules ‘specifically regulating the development of any AI model.” This legislation has not been formally introduced in Congress.

Many of the efforts described above have drawn [criticism](https://rollcall.com/2026/06/04/bipartisan-ai-draft-proposes-three-year-preemption-of-state-laws/) from commentators focused on AI safety; Brad Carson, the president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, wrote that the Great American AI Act’s preemption of state laws would be “a generational mistake,”; Brendan Steinhauser, the CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI, wrote that the draft Act fell “short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI.”

Historical baseline:
As of August 2026, no federal statute or regulation bars states from establishing stricter AI requirements than federal law, and no final court ruling has displaced a substantive category of state AI regulation.

Resolution criteria:
* This question resolves positively at the first documented instance after August 26, 2026 in which the U.S. federal government, by binding statute, regulation, or final federal court order, preempts or invalidates state AI laws, thereby legally barring states from enforcing a substantive category of AI regulation.
* This question concerns ceiling preemption only (i.e., preemption setting a federal maximum that states may not exceed, as opposed to a floor they remain free to exceed with stricter policies of their own). A statute or regulation or federal court order which preempts or invalidates state AI laws will not resolve this question if states retain authority to impose stricter or additional AI requirements than the federal baseline. Minimum standards set at the federal level only count toward the resolution of this question if they bar a state or states from adding to or exceeding federal standards.
* The preempted category must extend across application domains (e.g., barring states from imposing obligations on general-purpose AI models or AI systems generally). Federal preemption confined to a single regulated sector (motor vehicles, medical devices, credit reporting, aviation, communications platforms) does not resolve this question, regardless of how large that sector is or how much AI activity it covers.
* Actions that assert preemption authority or direct litigation toward it do not count unless and until they produce binding displacement of state law.
* Preliminary injunctions in individual cases do not count; the displacing action must be operative law.
* The action must prevent state authority over a substantive category of AI development or deployment regulation. Narrow state carve-outs in laws otherwise preventing state authority would not prevent the resolution of this question; likewise, measures limited to narrow areas of regulation would not resolve the question.
* A temporary statutory freeze or moratorium on state AI regulation would count toward the resolution of this question while in force, even if it is not reauthorized later.
* Instances in which federal funding is conditioned on state compliance with federal authority on regulation would not resolve this question unless the other criteria listed above are satisfied.
* If there is a reasonable dispute about whether an action meets these criteria, FRI will consult at least three qualified experts in AI governance or regulatory law to reach a resolution by majority vote.

P3. Pre-Release Authorization for Frontier Models

Summary: A binding requirement that frontier models be vetted and authorized before release, imposed by a US federal body or by an international body.

Part (a) is assumed: A US federal body holds pre-release authorization power

Background:
A federal pre-deployment licensing gate for frontier AI has been pursued through several channels but has not been enacted. In Congress, Senators Blumenthal and Hawley's 2023 [Bipartisan Framework for a U.S. AI Act](https://www.blumenthal.senate.gov/newsroom/press/release/blumenthal-and-hawley-announce-bipartisan-framework-on-artificial-intelligence-legislation) called for a licensing regime administered by an independent oversight body with authority to audit applicants, but was never introduced as a bill. In September 2025, the same senators introduced the [Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/2938/text), which would require developers to submit advanced AI systems to the Department of Energy before deployment, mandatory disclosure rather than a licensing decision, but it has not passed. In June 2026, the White House's [Executive Order 14409](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/06/promoting-advanced-artificial-intelligence-innovation-and-security/) created a voluntary pre-release review framework for "covered frontier models" while explicitly disclaiming any "mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement." That same month, the Commerce Department [required a license](https://fortune.com/2026/06/16/trump-administration-licensing-regime-for-frontier-ai-models-ad-hoc-and-opaque-eye-on-ai/) for the export or transfer of two Anthropic frontier models on national-security grounds, functioning as a de facto deployment gate through export-control authority rather than an AI-specific licensing statute.

Internationally, proposals have centered on inspection and verification rather than authorization. In May 2023, OpenAI leaders [argued](https://openai.com/index/governance-of-superintelligence/) that efforts above a capability or compute threshold should be subject to an international authority able to inspect systems, require audits, test for compliance with safety standards, and place restrictions on degrees of deployment; UN Secretary-General António Guterres subsequently [backed](https://www.reuters.com/technology/un-chief-backs-idea-global-ai-watchdog-like-nuclear-agency-2023-06-12/) an International Atomic Energy Agency-style body.

Historical baseline:
As of August 2026, no enacted federal statute, regulation, or executive order requires a license, approval, or other affirmative government authorization before a frontier model may be deployed in the United States. A voluntary pre-release review framework (EO 14409) is in operation and expressly disclaims mandatory licensing, and export-control action has restricted deployment of individual models on a case-by-case basis, but neither establishes pre-deployment licensing as operative law. The only enacted US laws directed at frontier model safety are state transparency and incident-reporting regimes, which impose no approval requirement.

No international body holds authorization power over frontier model release; existing multilateral AI bodies are advisory.

Resolution criteria:
* This question resolves positively at the first documented instance after August 26, 2026 in which a documented, binding measure requires developers of frontier models, as a class, to obtain affirmative authorization from a US federal or intergovernmental body before any such model may be released, deployed, or otherwise made externally available, and that requirement has taken effect. It must satisfy the following criteria, as well as the below bullets covering part (a) and (b) of this question separately:

P4. Strict Liability

Summary: A US federal statute treating frontier model training and deployment as an abnormally dangerous activity subject to strict liability (i.e., a regime under which a developer is liable for harms its models cause without the injured party having to prove the developer was careless or the model defective). The statute permits damages reflecting the expected magnitude of unrealized harm the conduct made more likely and requires developers to be insured for their liability.

Background:
[Strict liability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strict_liability) is an exception to the ordinary rule that a plaintiff must prove the defendant was at fault. For a narrow set of activities courts classify as "abnormally dangerous" (e.g., storing hazardous chemicals, keeping wild animals), a plaintiff need only show the activity caused the harm, and reasonable care is no defense. Congress has enacted comparable regimes by statute for hazardous industries, including [CERCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superfund), the [Oil Pollution Act of 1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_Pollution_Act_of_1990), and the [Price-Anderson Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price%E2%80%93Anderson_Nuclear_Industries_Indemnity_Act), which pair strict liability with mandatory financial responsibility scaled to the risk. No US jurisdiction has extended this category to AI; existing AI litigation proceeds on products liability and negligence theories, which retain a defect or fault element. A [leading articulation](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/5e7TrmH7mBwqpZ6ek/tort-law-can-play-an-important-role-in-mitigating-ai-risk) of this policy is Gabriel Weil's, which pairs strict liability with insurance requirements that scale with dangerous model capabilities and punitive damages addressing uninsurable risks.

Historical baseline:
As of August 2026, no US jurisdiction has classified frontier AI training or deployment as an abnormally dangerous activity by statute or controlling judicial holding, no US law requires AI developers to carry liability insurance, and no US jurisdiction authorizes punitive damages against AI developers absent a showing of malice or recklessness.

Resolution criteria:
* This question resolves positively at the first documented instance after August 26, 2026 in which all three of the following are simultaneously operative federally across the United States and applicable to all frontier developers:
  * strict liability for harms caused by frontier AI models
  * a liability insurance requirement scaled to assessed model capabilities
  * punitive damages available without proof of malice or recklessness in cases where realized harm is correlated with a larger unrealized catastrophic outcome.
* Only federal law resolves this question. A qualifying instrument is a federal statute in force, or a regulation promulgated under a federal statute that authorizes it.
  * State statutes, state common law developments, and state regulatory action do not count toward any element, whether individually or in combination. Federal court decisions applying state tort law do not count, including a federal court's characterization of frontier AI training or deployment as an abnormally dangerous activity where that characterization rests on state law.
* The strict liability element requires that a plaintiff be able to recover for harms caused by a frontier model without proving negligence, defect, or unreasonable design. Physical harm to persons or property must be within the scope of recoverable harm; a regime that also reaches economic loss, or that reaches economic loss in addition to physical harm, still counts. A regime confined to economic loss, privacy, discrimination, or reputational harm does not count.
  * A regime in which the developer may escape liability by demonstrating compliance with a standard of care, an approved safety framework, or industry best practice does not count.
  * A federal products liability standard that requires a design defect or failure to warn does not count.
* The insurance element requires that federal law condition training or deployment on demonstrating liability insurance, self-insurance, surety, or equivalent financial assurance, in an amount that varies as a function of model capability, training compute, or evaluation results. A flat, uniform, or de minimis requirement does not count, nor does a requirement scaled solely to developer revenue, valuation, or headcount. Voluntary coverage, insurer underwriting practices, and industry commitments do not count.

  * Punitive damages must be available even in the absence of malice, fraud, oppression, or reckless disregard.
  * The regime must permit awards to reflect the expected magnitude of harm the conduct made more likely, including catastrophic harm that did not in fact occur.
* A regime whose covered model definition, exemptions, or carve-outs exclude one or more of the largest US frontier developers by training compute does not resolve this question.
* If there is a reasonable dispute about whether an action meets these criteria, FRI will consult at least three qualified experts in tort law or AI governance to reach a resolution by majority vote.

label: Opus 5

rationale: I read the ladders literally ("one or more incidents cumulatively"), so low rungs are driven by aggregation of already-occurring AI-enabled harm rather than by a single catastrophe: recorded deepfake-fraud losses ran $2.5B in 2025 and $764M in H1 2026, IBM's 2026 breach report puts one in four malicious breaches as AI-enabled at ~$6M each, Interpol logs $442B of global fraud being "industrialised" by AI, and FRI's LEAP experts expect AI to add tens of billions per year to US-reported cybercrime by 2031 — so $220M and $2.2B cumulative are near-certain/likely inside 6–12 months, $22B is a coin flip, and I discounted higher rungs by ~35–70% weight on a stricter single-incident reading a resolver might apply. Death-defined rungs are anchored on much thinner evidence: no AI-related epidemic has ever occurred (takeoff.watch puts a government-confirmed AI-material synthesis at 34–56% and ≥10 linked deaths at only 7–11% by 2031), the first AI-autonomous drone killing (3 civilians, July 2026) and the Minab strike show military AI is the nearest mass-casualty vector, and confirmed loss-of-control events so far (Hugging Face, AISI's Mythos 5 runs, Anthropic's four breakout incidents, ~1,600 logged 2026 incidents) caused essentially no economic damage. For the catastrophe/extinction tier I anchor on FRI LEAP Wave 9 (AI catastrophe ≥10% of population: 1%/5%/10% by 2030/2050/2100 in a rapid world, 15% any-cause by 2100) and XPT (AI extinction 0.38% superforecasters vs 3% experts), landing near the rapid-progress end because GPT-6 Astra already self-declares Critical cyber capability, an "automated research intern" exists, and Chinese/open models trail by ~4 months — hence ~7% AI catastrophe and ~2.8% AI extinction by 2100, with disempowerment (25% by 2100) the most likely severe outcome. Policy conditions move tails, not the diffuse low rungs: preemption and status quo raise tail risk modestly (+5–18%), US-only compute caps, pre-release licensing or strict liability cut it ~20–30%, and the US–China bundle (P5) cuts it ~55% since much harm flows from open-weight and foreign models and from already-deployed systems. Capability conditions matter most at 2028–2050 tails (p90 ≈ 2.2x p50, p10 ≈ 0.55x) and barely at all where probabilities are already saturated.

label: GPT-5.5 Pro
rationale: I anchored the cross-cutting and high-severity AI risks mainly on AIRO's September 2026 ensemble (e.g. ~0.47% AI catastrophe by 2030, 6% by 2050, 12.2% by 2100; general catastrophe ~1.1%, 8.5%, 18.5%), then blended downward toward superforecaster-style skepticism for literal extinction and upward for lower severity damage thresholds where cyber/fraud/scam and chatbot/misalignment incidents already have visible base rates. For bio I used the FRI LLM-enabled biorisk elicitation (median ~0.3% annual for a human-caused 100k-death/$1T event in 2028, with higher risk under advanced LLM capabilities and lower risk under safeguards) but reduced it for specifically AI-related and for extreme-transmissibility/extinction tails. For cyber I put high probability on $220M/$2.2B-scale AI-related campaigns over multi-year horizons, based on recent AI-assisted intrusion reports and FRI's cyber-risk elicitation, while keeping 100M+/extinction cyber deaths very low absent a coupled nuclear, infrastructure, or bio pathway. Policy condition multipliers reflect AIRO's direction and approximate magnitude: status quo/preemption raise risk; US-only controls reduce modestly; international compute caps/release gates, strict liability, and especially the bundle reduce more; capability conditions scale risk monotonically with early-2027 ECI. My ECI quantiles follow Epoch/AIRO's observed reasoning-era trend of roughly 14 ECI/year from 169.2 in early September 2026, with asymmetric uncertainty for another large jump by March 18, 2027.

results.title: AI Queries Raise Concerns Over a Potential New Biological Weapons Race
results.content:
## What AI Queries Involved Biological Research and Dual-Use Risks?

Anthropic disclosed five biology-related cases between December 2025 and August 2026 involving users who attempted to bypass safety controls while using Claude for sensitive research. The cases involved dual-use biology, including chikungunya, highly pathogenic avian influenza, orthopoxviruses, toxins, and venoms.

Anthropics could not determine whether the activities were intended to cause harm. That uncertainty remains central to the broader debate.

Similar research can support vaccines, drug discovery, and public-health preparedness while also creating potential misuse concerns as AI capabilities grow. [...] Reported AI queries involving sensitive pathogen research have intensified concerns about a biological weapons race, even though malicious intent remains unproven. The cases highlight how difficult it can be to separate science from potential misuse.

As AI capabilities grow, biosecurity safeguards will remain important, but experts disagree over how restrictive they should become. A balanced approach could combine access controls, DNA screening, model safeguards, and transparent reporting while preserving research.

Trust is foundational to customer relationships. As synthetic content becomes indistinguishable from authentic communication, verification and monitoring mechanisms must evolve accordingly.

## AI-Enabled Cyber Threats: Not Fully Autonomous — Yet

According to the report summarized by The Guardian, AI systems can now support attackers at various stages of cyber operations—from identifying targets to preparing malware. However, fully autonomous, end-to-end cyberattacks remain difficult because AI systems cannot yet execute extended, multi-stage tasks independently (The Guardian).

Nonetheless, reported incidents indicate high degrees of automation in certain operations.

### Enterprise Risk Considerations

Partial automation dramatically increases scale: [...] Individually, each development may appear manageable:

 Improved reasoning
 Synthetic content proliferation
 AI-assisted cyber activity
 Oversight evasion
 Expanding autonomy

Collectively, they create compounding systemic risk.

 Improved reasoning increases automation.
 Automation increases scale.
 Scale amplifies error and misuse.
 Oversight becomes more complex.
 Trust erodes faster.

Risk timelines are compressing.

## What Businesses Should Be Cautious Of Now

The International AI Safety Report does not predict catastrophe. It highlights accelerating capability growth alongside expanding areas of uncertainty.

# AI Security Report 2026

July 14, 2026

For years, the cyber security industry tracked AI as a force multiplier: something that made existing attack techniques faster, cheaper, and more accessible. That framing was accurate. But the Annual AI Security Report 2026 from Check Point Research documents a transition that goes further. AI has crossed from assistant to operator. Where it once helped attackers prepare, it now runs the operation.

Title: A Model for the Probability of Nuclear War | Global Catastrophic Risk Institute
# A Model for the Probability of Nuclear War. by Seth Baum, Robert de Neufville, Anthony Barrett. The probability of nuclear war is a major factor in many important policy questions, but it has gotten little scholarly attention. This paper presents a model for calculating the total probability of nuclear war. The model is based on 14 interrelated scenarios for how nuclear war can break out, covering perhaps the entire range of nuclear war scenarios. Scenarios vary based on factors including whether a state intends to make a first strike attack, whether the nuclear attack is preceded by a conventional war or a non-war crisis, whether escalation is intentional or inadvertent, the presence of false alarms of various types, and the presence of non-war nuclear detonations such as nuclear terrorism. As a first step towards quantifying the probability of nuclear war using the model, the paper also includes a dataset of historical incidents that might have threatened to turn into nuclear war. 60 historical incidents are included, making it perhaps the largest such dataset currently available. The paper also includes background information about probabilistic analysis and modeling to help readers understand how to think about the probability of nuclear war, including new theory for the decision to initiate nuclear war. results.content:
Title: Uncertain Human Consequences in Asteroid Risk Analysis and the Global Catastrophe Threshold | Global Catastrophic Risk Institute
# Uncertain Human Consequences in Asteroid Risk Analysis and the Global Catastrophe Threshold. Asteroid collision is probably the most well-understood global catastrophic risk. This paper shows that it’s not so well understood after all, due to uncertainty in the human consequences. This finding matters both for asteroid risk and for the wider study of global catastrophic risk. If asteroid risk is not well understood, then neither are other risks such as nuclear war and pandemics. In addition to our understanding of the risks, two other important issues are at stake. One is policy for asteroids (and likewise for other risks). The paper argues that greater uncertainty about the human consequences demands more aggressive asteroid risk reduction, in order to err on the safe side of avoiding catastrophe. Also at stake are which risks to prioritize, including extinction risks vs. Uncertainty in the fate of survivors can be a reason to prioritize sub-extinction risks similarly to extinction risks. This issue is also discussed in the recent paper Long-Term Trajectories of Human Civilization. The paper includes some discussion of the prospect of nuclear war triggered by asteroid collisions. Automated Forecasts of Catastrophic Risks Jason Abaluck∗ Ezra Karger∗ Nick Merrill∗ Philip E. Tetlock∗ Eva Vivalt∗ Bridget Williams∗ September 2026 Abstract People hold radically different views about the risk of global catastrophe from AI. We present evidence that AI systems can help adjudicate these views: frontier models now predict binary real-world events about as accurately as the best humans (“superforecasters”) and predict rare events in complex simulations increasingly well as AI capabilities improve (Spearman ρ = +0.85). We introduce the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO), a regularly updated panel of frontier models’ forecasts of catastrophic risk. At time of writing, the panel’s median forecast that AI causes a catastrophe leading to the death of at least 10% of humans is 0.47% by 2030, 6.0% by 2050, and 12.2% by 2100. The AI-catastrophe median is about 45% of the all-cause median by 2030 and 71% by 2050. We also elicit cumulative incident forecasts on a standardized death-and-damage scale. At the highest threshold (equivalent to one billion deaths), misalignment is the highest risk, followed by cyber and biological risks. Estimates of risk are contingent on AI capabilities: conditioning on each model’s own 90th-percentile estimate of frontier capability by March 2027 raises its AI-catastrophe forecast by 2030 by 2.21×. Models forecast that compute caps and pre-release reviews would meaningfully reduce risk, although these policies would have other costs that we do not model. Because our panel’s accuracy rises with the same capability growth that likely drives potential AI risks, these forecasts are most informative in precisely the future worlds where AI risk is highest.
∗Authors listed alphabetically. Jason Abaluck: Yale University and the National Bureau of Economic Research; Ezra Karger: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago; Nick Merrill: Forecasting Research Institute and University of California, Berkeley; Philip E. Tetlock: University of Pennsylvania; Eva Vivalt: University of Toronto; Bridget Williams: Forecasting Research Institute and University of Oxford.
This work was funded by a grant from Coefficient Giving.
The views expressed in this paper do not necessarily represent the views of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago or the Federal Reserve System.
1 1 Introduction People differ wildly in their assessment of catastrophic risks posed by AI. AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Elon Musk estimate a 10–25% chance of catastrophic outcomes including human extinction within the next few decades (Morrone, 2025; Tangalakis-Lippert, 2024), while aca-demic experts express a wide range of views; Geoffrey Hinton (2018 Turing Award; 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics) gives similarly high estimates of extinction risk (Milmo, 2024) while Yann LeCun (2018 Turing Award) places this probability below that of extinction from an asteroid hitting the earth (< 0.001% over the next millennium) (LeCun, 2023). Surveys of AI experts and superforecasters in 2022–2023 placed the probability of AI-caused extinction by 2100 at 3–5% and 0.4%, respectively (Karger et al., 2023; Grace et al., 2025), although both groups underestimated subsequent AI capability progress (Kuˇ cinskas et al., 2025). If true risk is sub-stantial, mitigating it could be the single most important public policy priority in human history, especially if this could be done without sacrificing the substantial possible benefits of AI (Jones, 2024). On the other hand, if the lowest-end estimates are right, costly slowdowns proposed by many lab leaders and pundits would achieve little while stymying potential scientific innovation and economic growth.
We believe this debate is missing a key input: forecasts from frontier large language models.
The best models now approach superforecaster levels in the accuracy of their predictions; models are rapidly becoming more capable, and more capable models make better forecasts (Karger et al., 2025; ForecastBench, 2026). We show below that more capable models also make better forecasts of low-probability events in simulated environments. This evidence does not prove that more capable models can accurately forecast catastrophic risks, but it is suggestive. If models become more capable in ways that lead to increased risks from AI, model forecasting should likewise improve, providing increasingly accurate warning signs.
If the probability of catastrophe does spike and regulators or policymakers determine that coordination and decisive action are needed, accurate forecasts could act as a bellwether, alerting frontier labs and governments about which actions would most clearly mitigate risk. Forecasts could also act as a Schelling point, helping to solve coordination problems between competing AI companies or countries by establishing common knowledge of status quo risks and policy counterfactuals.
We introduce the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO), a dashboard showing frontier model forecasts of various types of catastrophic risk. Our main definition of a catastrophe is an event that leads to the death of at least 10% of the global population within a short period of time (five years). Our dashboard includes top-line forecasts of overall catastrophic risk and catastrophic risk from AI specifically. It also includes severity-threshold forecasts for AI-related biosecurity, cybersecurity, and misalignment incidents. In the domain-specific forecasts, each threshold can be reached through deaths (or equivalent morbidity) or economic damages. We report separate forecasts from various frontier models, as well as an ensemble forecast that subsets to models with the highest score on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), a measure of general AI capabilities that strongly correlates with real-world forecasting ability.
Figure 1 shows two views of the dashboard: forecasts of AI catastrophe over time and forecasts of frontier AI capability alongside human forecasts and a trend projection.
2 Our top-line findings are: 1. The ensemble of models places the probability of any catastrophic event (AI or non-AI) at 1.1% by 2030 (models span 0.7–1.6%), 8.5% by 2050 (3.2–11.0%), and 18.5% by 2100 (7.8–28.0%); the corresponding AI-catastrophe medians are 0.47%, 6.0%, and 12.2%, respectively.
2. At one billion deaths or equivalent morbidity, misalignment has the highest median among the three domain-specific categories at the 2030, 2050 and 2100 horizons (0.29% by 2030, 4.8% by 2050, 9.1% by 2100). Cyber incidents and AI-related human-caused epidemics are nearly tied at this threshold in 2030 and 2050; by 2100, their medians are 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively.
3. The ensemble median probability of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2030 falls from 0.47% unconditionally to 0.21% when each model conditions on its own 10th-percentile estimate of frontier capability in March 2027, and rises to 1.2% at its own 90th percentile. # Forecasting LLM-enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards

Forecasting LLM-enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards

This forecasting study on biological risks from large language models (LLMs) examined expert views on AI-enabled biosecurity threats. The study saw 46 biosecurity and biology experts, along with 22 superforecasters, predict how advancing LLM capabilities might increase the risk of a human-caused epidemic.

## Abstract

Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted excitement about their usefulness for beneficial research, but also concern about potential biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject-matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. The median expert predicted a 0.3% baseline annual risk of a human-caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top-performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs have already crossed this performance threshold. The median respondent thought that this would not happen until after 2030. More encouragingly, experts reduced their risk forecast close to baseline (0.4%) conditional on the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening.

Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong improvements in biological capabilities and now outperform PhD-level experts on a variety of biology benchmarks.[1](#cc8cf5c1-7adc-4539-8bf1-a46acabc2c04) Similarly, LLMs have shown early promise in providing scientific tutoring[2](#a4175eec-98fe-4a65-ad16-96b44d7a0260) and assisting with the conduct of scientific research.[3](#880d53e1-1040-4f1c-b505-9ac79daa2454) While there are still clear limitations to how useful LLMs can be in science,[4](#a06a3646-f62a-464b-aec7-4a720dd7167c) there is a clear trend that new models are more capable than their predecessors.

Numerous observers—including leaders of frontier AI companies—recognize both the benefits and risks that such capabilities could bring in the near future.[5](#0442a866-a327-4cd7-aa62-606408cb9ad3) OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic have all released policies to prevent LLM misuse of biology and run capability evaluations on new models ahead of their commercial deployment.[6](#f403dcd0-9794-40af-8560-184dcaeef4a9) Recently, Anthropic announced that it provisionally implemented a stronger security standard for its latest model release, since it could not rule out that it might significantly assist with CBRN-weapons-related tasks of concern.[7](#e48f546e-9258-4240-a4c0-8698307f1550) OpenAI has announced that it is preparing similar mitigations.[8](#9894317f-d068-4c25-ba29-9c83d0d65094) However, it is still unclear which empirical evaluation results would indicate that LLMs present a meaningful increase in risk.[9](#ca3afd3a-bfdb-4747-9b60-de3ca69c3f84) It is also unclear what sorts of mitigation measures would then be most helpful in reducing such risk while preserving the power of the models to advance scientific work.

Forecasting the probability of biological threats is challenging due to the rarity of such events and the complex interplay of technical, social, and political factors involved.[10](#e05cf7f2-dd1b-41eb-ae6d-bf59dda468aa) Previous surveys have found a wide range of views.
